36: Psalm 22 is not merely a record of anguish; it is the map that traces the path from the dust of Golgotha to the splendor of the Universal Throne.

This Psalm begins with the cry of abysmal abandonment—*"My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"* (Psalm 22:1)—yet it concludes with shouts of victory and hope: *"All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations will bow down before him..."* — Psalm 22:27 (NIV). The suffering of our Lord was not a tragic detour in God's plan, nor a momentary failure of justice; rather, it was the blood-bought price that purchased the worship of every tribe and nation.

Picture the scene of the crucifixion. In the eyes of men, it was the end of a Galilean dream; to the angels, it was the fulfillment of the most ancient promise. Psalm 22, penned a thousand years before Christ, divides masterfully into two movements: the groans of the Crucified (vv. 1–21) and the songs of the Glorified (vv. 22–31). It is what theologians call the "Cross" and the "Crook" (or "Scepter").

Van Groningen observes that Psalm 22 contains details of messianic suffering that transcend David's personal experience and find direct fulfillment in the Passion of Christ, as recorded across the four Gospels (GRONINGEN, 1995, chaps. 11–12). Eichrodt acknowledges that Psalm 22, "in accordance with the preaching concerning the suffering servant of God, develops 'ideas relating to the messianic execution of salvation'" (EICHRODT, cited in GRONINGEN, 1995, p. 84).

As the *Beacon Bible Commentary* aptly observes, the christological intention of this poem is undeniable, being quoted seven times in the New Testament. The suffering described therein was no accident, but a divine "it was necessary" (*edei*); it was fitting that the Christ should suffer so that He might enter into His glory and bring many sons with Him. The "Man of Sorrows" sowed in tears so that the whole world might reap in joy.

The climax of this prophecy bursts forth in verses 27 and 28: *"All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations will bow down before him, for dominion belongs to the Lord"* (Psalm 22:27–28, NIV).
37: Hebrews 1:8–9 directly quotes this passage in reference to Christ. We are presented with a bridal hymn, a royal *epithalamium* recorded in Psalm 45. At the heart of this Psalm, the psalmist—with the pen of a skillful writer—drops the veil of humanity and proclaims something that makes the earth tremble: *"Your throne, O God, will last for ever and ever; a scepter of justice will be the scepter of your kingdom"* (Psalm 45:6, NIV). Notice carefully: the psalmist addresses the King as **"O God"**! Here, the shadow of an earthly monarch vanishes to make way for the substance of the Messiah, the Anointed One who unites within Himself the frailty of our flesh and the immutability of Deity. Unlike the kingdoms of this world, which are born in purple and die in the dust of history, the dominion of Christ is not temporal, but Eternal.

The God-King is He who has "loved righteousness and hated wickedness." The true character of a ruler is revealed by what he loves and what he abominates, and the immaculate holiness of Christ is the bedrock upon which His eternal throne stands unshakable.

The text proceeds by declaring that God anointed this King with the "oil of joy" above His companions (Psalm 45:7). In Old Testament culture, anointing with fragrant oil was a hallmark of hospitality, favor, and above all, royal investiture. But why did Christ receive more joy? Because He was the only descendant of David who perfectly fulfilled every condition of obedience that the Father demanded.
39: Jesus asked this very question to the Pharisees in Matthew 22:41–46, quoting Psalm 110:1, and "no one could say a word in reply."
40: The Epistle to the Hebrews (chaps. 5–7) extensively expounds Melchizedek's priesthood as a typology of Christ.

Van Groningen devotes an extensive study to Psalm 110, which he considers "the most significant messianic revelation in the Poetic Writings," uniting the offices of king and priest in a single person (GRONINGEN, 1995, p. 356).
41: King Ahaz, heir to the throne of David yet not to David's faith, saw on the horizon the dust kicked up by the armies of Aram (Syria) and Israel. The sacred record recounts that the heart of the king and his people shook *"as the trees of the forest are shaken by the wind"* (Isaiah 7:2, NIV). It is amidst this backdrop of emotional collapse that the prophet Isaiah is sent with an offer of relief that defies human logic.

The Lord, in His astounding patience, offers Ahaz a blank check: *"Ask the Lord your God for a sign, whether in the deepest depths or in the highest heights"* (Isaiah 7:11, NIV). Yet Ahaz, cloaked in a simulated piety that was nothing more than hardened unbelief, rejects divine aid to seek the rotten alliance of Assyria.

Confronted by the king's hypocritical silence, God Himself speaks. He does not revoke the promise; He expands it for eternal generations: *"Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: The virgin will conceive and give birth to a son, and will call him Immanuel"* (Isaiah 7:14, NIV).
The prophesied sign was not merely a prediction for the days of Ahaz, but a divine wonder that would transcend the very laws of nature.

The Hebrew term *'almâ* denotes a young maiden of marriageable age who is sexually pure, and the Septuagint, centuries before Bethlehem, translated it as *parthenos*—the exact Greek term defining absolute virginity. Had the birth not been virginal, it could not have truly served as a miraculous sign from the Most High to the house of David.

The birth of Jesus was no ordinary biological event, but the invasion of time by Eternity. As biblical scholarship rightly observes, this event is the central theme of the entire Gospel: *"The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us"* (John 1:14, NIV). If the first Adam was formed from the dust of the ground without the intervention of a human father, the Second Adam, our Redeemer, had to be conceived in an even more glorious manner, so that His rest would be divine and His humanity perfect.

Behold now the figure of Mary. A young woman of Nazareth, a town of which Nathanael famously asked: *"Can anything good come from Nazareth?"* (John 1:46, NIV). Mary was chosen not for earthly nobility, but by the sovereign grace of the Father. She was "highly favored"—a redeemed sinner who, like all of us, stood in need of a Savior, as she herself proclaimed in her *Magnificat*: *"My spirit rejoices in God my Savior"* (Luke 1:47, NIV).

When the angel Gabriel announced the impossible to her, her response was not the skepticism of Zechariah, but the holy awe of faith: *"How will this be," Mary asked the angel, "since I am a virgin?"* (Luke 1:34, NIV). The angel then unveiled Heaven’s method: *"The Holy Spirit will come on you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you"* (Luke 1:35, NIV). Beloved reader, notice the beauty of this "overshadowing": the very same Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation was now hovering over Mary’s womb to inaugurate the New Creation. Mary embraced the burden that would bring relief to the world with the sweetest words a mortal could utter: *"May your word to me be fulfilled"* (Luke 1:38, NIV).

The virgin birth ensures that Jesus is, at once, the Son of God and the Son of Man. He had to be man in order to suffer in our stead, and God so that His sacrifice would possess infinite worth. He is the true *Yehoshua*—"Yahweh Saves"—who came to save His people not *in* their sins, but *from* their sins.
42: Isaiah not only heralds the birth, but unlocks the royal treasury of deity to display the royal titles of this Ruler. **1. Wonderful Counselor:** He is a personal marvel, a God who requires no earthly advisors because He possesses the fullness of omniscience. Under His reign, the weary soul finds not mere commands, but the profound, extraordinary wisdom of One who knows every labyrinth of our heart; **2. Mighty God:** Upon the sacred terrain of the Hebrew, we read *El-Gibbor*—the Divine Warrior or Mighty Champion. He is not merely endowed with strength; the essential nature of deity tabernacles within Him, ensuring that His omnipotence crushes every enemy that seeks to rob His people of rest; **3. Everlasting Father:** The term *Abi’ad* portrays Him who, as the sovereign Architect of creation, nurtures His subjects with the tender care of a father devoted to the eternal destiny of his children. Jesus is the "Eternal Contemporary" who walks through the centuries to shepherd the flock He Himself created; **4. Prince of Peace:** He is the *Sar-Shalom*. Soul relief, dear reader, is not simply the absence of warfare, but the positive presence of *shalom*—a rich, harmonious, and flourishing state of well-being that only the true Rest-Giver can bestow.
43: Regarding Isaiah 53:10–11, it is observed that seeing His "offspring" and the "prolonging of his days" following death and atonement necessarily point toward the resurrection.

Let us examine this fourfold revelation of the Person of Christ. **I.** The First Song: The Character of the Chosen One (Isaiah 42:1–9)—the official presentation of the Servant by the Father Himself: *"Here is my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen one in whom I delight"* (Isaiah 42:1, NIV). As the *Willmington's Guide to the Bible* rightly highlights, Jesus is the Servant chosen, beloved, and spiritually endowed by God. He comes not with the clamor of Alexander's armies nor the pomp of Caesars. The hallmark of His governance is exquisite meekness. He will not shout in the streets or raise His voice to court popularity; **II.** The Second Song: The Calling and Light to the Gentiles (Isaiah 49:1–7)—the Servant recounts His divine commission: *"Before I was born the Lord called me; from my mother’s womb he has spoken my name"* (Isaiah 49:1, NIV). This is a transparent allusion to the virgin birth and the predetermined mission of Christ. He was concealed within God's quiver, a polished arrow in Nazareth, awaiting the appointed hour to be loosed against the darkness; **III.** The Third Song: The School of Suffering (Isaiah 50:4–11)—at this juncture, the Servant's soliloquy turns into dark tones of physical torment and moral indignity. He professes an "instructed tongue" to sustain the weary, yet the price of that word is submission to violent abuse: *"I offered my back to those who beat me, my cheeks to those who pulled out my beard; I did not hide my face from mocking and spitting"* (Isaiah 50:6, NIV); **IV.** The Fourth Song: The Great Exchange (Isaiah 52:13—53:12)—here, the Servant stands forth as the Martyr and the Atoning Sacrifice. Isaiah portrays the Messiah as the "Man of Sorrows," someone whose visage was so disfigured by torture that He scarcely retained human form. But why such agony? The answer is the bedrock of the Gospel: Substitution. *"Surely he took up our pain and bore our suffering"* (Isaiah 53:4, NIV).

The most sublime detail is the closing paradox. The Servant dies, is buried in a rich man's tomb, yet the prophetic voice boldly proclaims: *"He will see his offspring and prolong his days"* (Isaiah 53:10, NIV). Beloved reader, how can a dead man see descendants unless He rises bodily from the grave? The Servant’s exaltation—being raised, lifted up, and highly exalted—is the definitive proof that His atoning sacrifice was fully accepted, and that the invitation to divine rest is forever sealed in blood and victory.
44: Daniel was enveloped in the quiet of the Babylonian night as the Holy Spirit unveiled to him the bloody destiny of nations. He envisioned four extraordinarily fierce beasts—winged lions, ravenous bears, and swift leopards—representing the succession of world empires: Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome. Yet, just as the ferocity of the fourth beast reached its terrifying pinnacle, the scene shifted dramatically from earthly turmoil to the celestial courtroom. Daniel beheld the "Ancient of Days" seated upon a throne of flaming fire, encircled by myriads of heavenly beings.

At the epicenter of this ineffable glory, there stepped forward One shining with an entirely different light: *"there before me was one like a son of man, coming with the clouds of heaven"* (Daniel 7:13, NIV). As biblical scholars readily note, Jesus applied this very title to Himself no fewer than 81 times in the Gospels, uniting within His single person the frailty of our humanity and the absolute authority of Deity. Whereas human kingdoms rise clad in purple and crumble into the dust, the Son of Man receives from the Father an everlasting dominion that shall not pass away and a kingdom that will never be destroyed. Here lies the true rest of our soul: our Savior is no ephemeral sovereign, but the Eternal Monarch who rides the clouds to usher us into His rest.

**The Mystery of the Seventy Weeks** — Years later, Daniel, that tireless intercessor, was bent over the scrolls of Jeremiah, discerning the 70 years of exile, when the archangel Gabriel touched his shoulder with history’s greatest chronological disclosure: the **Seventy Weeks**. God was not merely forecasting the conclusion of a physical captivity, but uncovering the divine timeline for the eradication of the soul's rebellion.

These seventy weeks (490 prophetic years) were decreed with six magnificent objectives: to finish transgression, to put an end to sin, to atone for wickedness, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the Most Holy Place. As biblical chronologists demonstrate, the prophetic clock began ticking on March 14, 445 BC, when King Artaxerxes issued the decree permitting Nehemiah to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem.

But observe what transpires after the sixty-two weeks: *"the Anointed One will be put to death"* (Daniel 9:26, NIV). The original Hebrew expression signifies that the Messiah would be "cut off" or "severed," as one eliminated by formal judicial sentence. Beloved, here beats the very heart of the Gospel call! The Messiah came not to be crowned by mortal hands in silk-draped palaces, but to be "cut off" upon the tree of shame.

The prophecy adds that He will *"have nothing"* (or *"be no more"*). In the sight of the world, it seemed like an absolute defeat; to the hordes of hell, it looked like the extinction of the Seed. Yet Jesus was not slain because His purpose had faltered; He died because the atonement of iniquity demanded the spotless blood of the Lamb. He was cut off from the land of the living so that we might never be cut off from the fellowship of the Father.

**The Grammatical Precision of Daniel 9:26 (*****Yikaret Mashiach*****)** — When scrutinizing the prophecy of the 70 Weeks in Daniel 9, the Hebrew term *yikaret* ("the Anointed One will be cut off and will have nothing") is of paramount significance. This verb stems from *karat*, the identical root employed throughout the Old Testament to denote the solemn ratification of an alliance ("cutting a covenant") by the shedding of sacrificial blood. This demonstrates exegetically that the Messiah's violent death was the very act whereby the New Covenant was cut in the exact fullness of time prophesied by Daniel.
45: Jesus Himself affirmed the typological character of Jonah's experience in Matthew 12:39–40. Christian scholarship observes that the Jonah typology operates on a threefold plane: (1) **Substitutive**, by surrendering his own life to the raging sea (the wrath of God) to rescue the Gentile sailors; (2) **Resurrectional**, as his three-day ordeal in the belly of the great fish followed by his delivery onto dry ground stands as the premier Old Testament emblem of the death, three-day burial, and bodily resurrection of the Messiah; and (3) **Missiological**, for it was only following this "resurrection" that the proclamation of divine grace and repentance reached Nineveh, prefiguring the Great Commission to herald the Gospel among all Gentile nations after Christ's resurrection.
46: Micah, the country prophet who, unlike the aristocratic Isaiah, spoke from the rustic pastures and directly to the downtrodden. Amidst his outcry against institutional injustice and the corruption of the elite, he proclaimed a promise that would sustain Israel's hope across more than seven centuries: *"But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come for me one who will be ruler over Israel, whose origins are from of old, from ancient times"* (Micah 5:2, NIV).

Bethlehem, whose Hebrew name (*Beyth Lechem*) translates literally to "House of Bread," was the appointed birthplace for Him who would proclaim Himself the "Bread of Life." It is specifically designated Bethlehem Ephrathah to distinguish it from the town of Bethlehem within the territory of Zebulun. Ephrathah was the ancient title of that region, synonymous with agricultural fruitfulness and the ancestral seat of David, the shepherd boy anointed king.

What renders this prophecy breathtaking is not simply its geographic pinpointing, but the transcendent nature of the promised Sovereign. Micah boldly asserts that His "origins" (His goings forth or manifestations) are *"from ancient times, from the days of eternity"* (Micah 5:2, NIV).

The Hebrew phrase "from the days of eternity" (*mîmê ‘ôlām*) attributes to the messianic ruler an eternal preexistence prior to His human incarnation, as articulated in Micah 5:2. Relying squarely on this prophecy, the Magi from the East were directed to Bethlehem, as recounted in Matthew 2:4–6.
47: Picture the year 520 BC atop Mount Moriah. The scene of the rebuilding of the Temple no longer boasts the gleaming marble and Ophir gold of Solomon's day, but is a construction site surrounded by ash and discouragement. When the foundations of the Second Temple were laid, a mingled sound echoed through the valleys of Jerusalem: the young shouted with joy, but the elders—those who still remembered the splendor of the first House—wept loudly.

In those aging eyes, the new structure seemed "like nothing" (Haggai 2:3, NIV). It lacked the five crown jewels of the first house: the Ark of the Covenant, the radiant cloud of the *Shekinah*, the celestial fire upon the altar, the Urim and Thummim, and the audible spirit of prophecy. Yet, amidst this apparent poverty, the Holy Spirit breathes a promise that shakes the very foundations of the cosmos.

The Lord, through the prophet Haggai, pierces the silence of despair with an oracle of absolute authority: *"This is what the Lord Almighty says: 'In a little while I will once more shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land. I will shake all nations, and what is desired by all nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory... The glory of this present house will be greater than the glory of the former house'"* (Haggai 2:6–9, NIV).

This prophesied "shaking" is not merely a geological tremor, but a spiritual and political revolution designed to prepare the way for the Messiah. The author of Hebrews confirms that this divine shaking removes what is transient and created so that only what is unshakable may remain: the Kingdom of Christ.

But who is the **"Desired of all nations"**? We clearly perceive in this expression the very Person of the Messiah. He is the hidden yearning of every human heart, the answer to the groaning of all cultures, and the true soul-rest that the nations long to find.
48: Matthew 27:3–10 records the literal fulfillment of the thirty pieces of silver as the price of Judas Iscariot's betrayal and the purchase of the "potter's field," linking directly to Zechariah 11:12–13.
49: It is observed in Zechariah 12:10 that Yahweh is, at once, the One who is pierced and the One who pours out the Spirit of grace—a profound proof pointing directly to the divine identity of the suffering Servant.

Picture the prophet Zechariah, herald of post-exilic hope, caught up in the Spirit to witness a scene that confounds the wisdom of this world. He sees not merely the reconstruction of stone ramparts, but the rebirth of hearts of flesh.

Zechariah records an oracle in which Yahweh Himself takes the floor and declares: *"And I will pour out on the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem a spirit of grace and supplication. They will look on me, the one they have pierced, and they will mourn for him as one mourns for an only child"* (Zechariah 12:10, NIV). Mark this well, Christian believers: it is the Lord God Almighty who declares that He Himself will be pierced! Biblical scholarship reveals that in the original Hebrew text, there appears the untranslated direct-object particle *'et* (את), formed by the letters *Aleph* and *Tav*, pointing directly to the Messiah, Jesus Christ, the Alpha and the Omega, who as Yahweh in flesh bears our wounds.

The piercing of God is no poetic metaphor; it is an epochal historical fact reverberating into eternity. While Israel pierced the Lord figuratively through centuries of stubborn rebellion, the literal and ultimate fulfillment took place when Roman soldiers drove a spear into Jesus’ side at Calvary. There, blood and water poured forth as a holy seal proving that the sacrifice was real and redemption complete.

The prophet foretells a profound national repentance. Under the outpouring of the *"spirit of grace"*, the people will no longer look upon the Messiah with scorn, but with bitter weeping, akin to grief for a firstborn son. As the *Beacon Bible Commentary* perceptively notes, this mourning commenced at the Cross, deepened at Pentecost, yet awaits its ultimate fulfillment at the Second Coming, when all Israel shall recognize the King they once spurned. Looking in faith upon the Pierced One is the only sovereign remedy capable of melting a stony heart into a heart of tender flesh.
50: Through a careful reading of Malachi 3:1–6 and 4:5–6, we identify the "messenger" as John the Baptist and the "Lord who will come to his temple" as the Messiah Himself. Jesus definitively confirmed this interpretation in Matthew 11:10 and Mark 1:2.

Malachi, whose very name signifies "my messenger," stands as the final watchman of the Old Testament. Often called the "Hebrew Socrates," he closes the Old Testament canon with searching questions that pierce through hypocrisy and luminous promises that illuminate the four centuries of prophetic silence that followed. To be sure, God's silence was not forgetfulness of His promises, but the necessary pause to awaken within the human soul a profound thirst for Him who is the Water of Life. Malachi does not leave the people in despair; he points toward a royal highway paved within the councils of eternity.

Malachi concludes his prophecy—and the entirety of the Old Testament—with a ringing note of warning and hope: *"See, I will send the prophet Elijah to you before that great and dreadful day of the Lord comes"* (Malachi 4:5, NIV). Beloved, this "Elijah" was not the Tishbite prophet reincarnated, but John the Baptist, the son of Zechariah, who heralded the kingdom in the "spirit and power of Elijah."

John the Baptist was also the "Malachi of the New Testament," the sacred link bridging the shadows of the law to the substance of grace. His commission was one of holy reconciliation: *"He will turn the hearts of the parents to their children, and the hearts of the children to their parents"* (Malachi 4:6, NIV). The soul-rest presented throughout this work is only realized when the heart is restored through the message of repentance that John thundered on the banks of the Jordan. Pointing his finger toward the horizon, he uttered the proclamation that should forever reverberate across our worship: *"Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!"* (John 1:29, NIV).
